title: Solar-cell Al2O3 field-effect passivation lines storage-node isolation
idea: Combine the negative fixed charge of ALD Al2O3 (used to passivate PERC solar cells) with DRAM isolation: line storage-node trenches with ALD Al2O3 so its built-in charge repels electrons from surfaces, suppressing surface-generation leakage and electron migration from aggressor rows. Buildable in a university nanofab: one ALD step and forming-gas anneal.
why: Retention tail and row hammer (facts 3, 9): field-effect passivation cuts surface generation currents by up to ~10x.

title: Self-restoring gain cell: one global pulse refreshes whole array
idea: Combine a gain cell with bootstrapped positive feedback: each 2T IGZO cell's storage node gates a second TFT that connects a pulsed restore rail back to the node, so pulsing the rail tops up only cells storing '1' (cells at '0' keep it off), refreshing the whole array in one pulse with no row activation or sensing. Buildable in a university nanofab: two-mask n-type IGZO TFT process.
why: Refresh bandwidth and energy (fact 3): removes the 10-20% bandwidth loss and per-row activation energy of refresh; risk is threshold loss needing a boosted rail.

title: Plate-line popcount probe checks row health without activating it
idea: Combine popcount checksums with segmented plate-line charge sensing: pulsing a row segment's plate and integrating the displaced charge gives its total stored charge (about the count of '1's); comparing it with a stored popcount detects leakage or hammer flips non-destructively, so only drifted rows are refreshed or scrubbed. Buildable in a university nanofab: segmented-plate MIM arrays with an off-chip integrator.
why: Destructive read and refresh (facts 3, 8, 9): refreshing only drifted rows could cut refresh activations >5x.

title: Sacrificial-etch air gaps isolate adjacent wordlines from hammer
idea: No EUV: at DUV pitch, a sacrificial carbon or oxide fill between buried wordlines is removed through DUV-defined vents and sealed, leaving air gaps (k=1) that cut aggressor-victim capacitive and trap coupling.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold ~3x and lower wordline capacitance (and CV2 energy) ~20%.

title: Goto-pair Esaki tunnel-diode bistable cell needs no refresh
idea: Two series interband tunnel diodes with negative differential resistance (the 1959 Goto pair), rebuilt as stacked SiGe epi under a vertical access transistor, form a bistable node. Retention goes as exp(Eb/kT), so a barrier >40 kT makes it unlimited. The design challenge is a valley current <=1 pA/cell (~5 mW standby per GB).
why: Refresh eliminated (fact 3). Endurance is unlimited because nothing moves atomically. 4-6F^2 without a capacitor.

title: Per-row variable-rate codes from factory cell-quality map
idea: Capacitorless cells spread widely in quality (read-transistor Vt, hole retention). At test, measure each row's raw BER and assign one of 4 code rates (none/SEC/DEC/t=4), stored as a 2-bit map in the controller. Good rows keep full capacity, and bad rows pay parity instead of being scrapped.
why: Yield/usable bits: +10-20% vs fixed worst-case ECC for capacitorless arrays.

title: Chemotactic co-aged references: multilevel cheap cells read against twins
idea: E. coli chemotaxis compares the present with a methylation-held memory of a moment ago rather than absolute levels; each row of 2-3-bit-per-cell cheap storage includes reference cells written at the same instant to each level, which leak and drift alongside the data, so sensing compares data to co-aged references and drift cancels.
why: Multiplies bits per cheap cell 2-3x where leak and drift normally forbid multilevel storage; a multiplier toward ~100x with stacked cheap tiers.

title: Aluminum nitride interlayers cool upper HBM dies to halve refresh
idea: Worse: stack 12-16 dies separated by thermally poor underfill so top dies run hottest and need 2x refresh. Flip: replace the underfill and bonding dielectric with thin AlN bonding layers (high thermal conductivity, Al and N only) that carry heat down to the base cooler.
why: Facts 3 and 6: 10-15 C lower peak die temperature halves leakage, keeping standard refresh at taller stack heights.

title: Band-to-band tunnel-FET access device gives attoamp-class off state
idea: Effect: interband (Zener) tunneling as the switching mechanism. A gated p-i-n tunnel FET replaces the access MOSFET; with no band overlap in the off state, leakage is limited by a reverse-biased junction (~1e-18 A, ~1000x below MOSFET tails), while its uA-class on-current still charges a 0.3 fF node in ~5 ns. The unidirectional conduction is handled by a split read/write gate design.
why: 10x density: 0.3 fF instead of 5 fF removes the capacitor module; a vertical TFET at 4F^2 stacked 6-8 tiers gives ~10x at similar cost.

title: Substitute polycrystalline HZO with templated single-grain epitaxial ferroelectric cells
idea: Grow HZO on a lattice-matched seed layer (e.g., YSZ or perovskite template) patterned so each cell is one oriented grain, removing grain-to-grain variation in coercive field and polarization.
why: Variability is the main FE error source at small cells; near-uniform cells cut raw BER and ECC overhead and allow scaling below 20 nm.

title: Replaceable base die carries ECC and refresh logic upgrades
idea: Rule: reliability logic must be upgradable without scrapping arrays. In stacked DRAM, the ECC engines, refresh scheduler, hammer defense and repair logic live in a base die joined through a reworkable interface. When better algorithms appear, the base die is swapped and the array dies are reused.
why: Fact 7: periphery (~49% of die) moves to a cheap logic node. Arrays outlive several generations of reliability logic.

title: Survivalist's go-bag: printed battery keeps memory alive through power faults
idea: A survivalist always keeps a go-bag packed: a thin-film zinc or lithium battery printed onto the DIMM or HBM carrier powers self-refresh for minutes after a PSU or rack power fault, so in-memory state (KV caches, in-memory databases) survives instead of being lost and recomputed.
why: Availability: avoids costly recomputation and checkpoint traffic and reduces the need for NVDIMM capacity, for cents per module.

title: Actuary's bronze tier: discounted relaxed-refresh memory for checkpointed jobs
idea: An actuary prices risk instead of eliminating it: cloud providers sell a 'bronze memory' NUMA node with relaxed refresh and lighter ECC at a 30-40% discount for jobs that checkpoint (ML training, batch analytics), opted in through an madvise-style flag, so lower-bin dies get a paying home.
why: Frees refresh bandwidth and lets the market absorb weaker cells, raising usable supply.

title: Refresh-free mode for data that dies before it decays
idea: Worse: refresh activation buffers and KV blocks that will be overwritten within milliseconds anyway. Flip: add a per-bank 'ephemeral' mode in which the controller declares regions whose data lives shorter than retention time (training activations, streaming buffers) and refresh is skipped; dies with poor retention tails are binned and sold for exactly these accelerator streaming roles.
why: Fact 3 refresh energy and yield: removes refresh on 30-60% of accelerator memory and turns retention-reject dies into sellable product.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes burn away dielectric weak spots
idea: Borrow film-capacitor self-healing and reverse what fails: the top electrode is ultrathin TiN from TiCl4/NH3 ALD (no WF6, no NF3 cleans), and a controlled overvoltage pulse at test vaporizes electrode around any leakage spot in the ZrO2, isolating the defect while ~99% of the capacitor stays active.
why: Retention tail from dielectric weak spots (higher with fluorine-free chamber cleans): converts leaky cells into good ones, shrinking the tail ~3-10x.

title: Canary replica cells at 60% Cs set local refresh
idea: Each subarray carries 64 deliberately weakened canary cells (60% of nominal Cs, written '1'). They see the same temperature, voltage, VRT and aging as the array but fail first. Background logic polls them, and the subarray's refresh rate relaxes until a canary fails, then steps up.
why: Refresh guardband (fact 3): physical tracking replaces worst-case margins, for 2-4x fewer refreshes.

title: Canary cells that decay first and call for refresh
idea: Ideal: memory that knows the instant it starts forgetting. Closest: every subarray carries a few deliberately weakened canary cells (narrower access FET, ~30% smaller Cs, written to '1'); a tiny comparator polls them and the subarray is refreshed only when its canaries droop past a guard threshold, so refresh follows real temperature, voltage and aging per subarray instead of the worst-case corner.
why: Fact 3: removes the 4-8x worst-case guard band in refresh rate; ~50-75% refresh energy cut in typical conditions.

title: Rest banks under deep reverse bias to undo chloride-gate BTI
idea: Reverse stress into recovery: chlorine-precursor TiN gates may add trap-driven Vt drift, so the controller rotates banks through scheduled recovery intervals with access transistors held at a deeper-than-standby negative gate bias, de-trapping charge before the leakage tail grows.
why: Prevents aging-driven growth of the leakage tail and keeps refresh intervals stable over the product life.

title: Telecom line coding: hammer-aware coset scrambling chosen per row
idea: Adapted from line codes (8b/10b, DC-balanced scramblers) that avoid patterns a channel handles badly: the memory controller tries 4 scrambler seeds on each row write and picks the one that minimizes known worst-case victim-aggressor stripe patterns (alternating data opposite to neighbors), storing the 2-bit seed index in spare ECC bits.
why: Row hammer and pattern-dependent retention (facts 3, 9): flip probability depends strongly on data pattern; avoiding worst patterns could raise the effective hammer threshold ~2-5x on existing chips with controller logic only.

title: Coset scrambling picks the least-coupled data pattern per row
idea: Po: memory that lies, but chooses its lie. On write, the controller tries four fixed scramble masks per row segment and stores the one minimizing charged-next-to-discharged adjacencies along bitline and passing-gate directions, recording the 2-bit mask ID in spare columns.
why: Data-pattern-dependent retention and coupling: the worst-case patterns that set the retention spec become rare, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh at ~0.4% capacity overhead.

title: Eliminate minority carriers: hole-free oxide channels make row hammer impossible
idea: Build arrays from wide-bandgap n-type oxides deposited at <=350 C, with no body contact and essentially no holes. The substrate charge-pumping and electron-migration mechanisms behind silicon row hammer then have no carrier population to act through. Qualify with hammer tests at 1M activations.
why: Could eliminate row hammer (fact 9) by physics, removing TRR and counter logic and their refresh bandwidth and simplifying the periphery (fact 7).

title: ALD alumina hydrogen-lock cap preserves interface passivation
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells/thin films: a thin ALD Al2O3 shell is deposited over the array right after the forming-gas anneal with domestic ALD tools and precursors, so hydrogen passivating gate-oxide and STI interface traps cannot outgas during later BEOL thermal steps.
why: Fewer active interface traps means a thinner trap-assisted leakage tail and fewer VRT cells, targeting ~2x longer refresh with no new tool class or imported material.

title: Deuterium anneal hardens access transistors against tail and hammer damage
idea: Effect: the giant isotope effect in Si-H/Si-D desorption. The final H2 forming anneal is replaced by a high-pressure D2 anneal; Si-D interface bonds are ~10-50x more resistant to hot-carrier and hammer-cycling desorption, so the interface-trap generation that grows VRT tails and hammer susceptibility over life slows sharply.
why: Lifetime reliability: keeps time-zero retention and hammer thresholds over years, so end-of-life guard bands shrink (~1.5-2x refresh relaxation). It is a drop-in process change.

title: Diagonal codeword interleaving makes row hammer statistically harmless
idea: Po: let the rows flip. Each codeword's bits are spread diagonally across 16-32 physical rows in several subarrays, so a fully hammered victim row contributes at most 1/16 of any codeword's errors; with 1%-capable codes an attacker must flip dozens of bits in many rows at once.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): effective threshold x10-100 with no per-row counters; mitigation logic area largely removed.

title: Half the capacitor: OS-toggled twin-row differential mode
idea: Imposed limit: build cells with half the capacitance (~2.5 fF, AR ~30:1). For pages flagged long-lived, two paired rows are activated together onto complementary bitlines to form a 2T2C differential bit, doubling signal and retention. Short-lived pages run single-ended at full density, and the OS chooses the mode per 2 MB region.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: shorter, cheaper capacitor pillars with fewer etch and deposition steps. Usable density adapts to how much data actually needs long retention.

title: Magnify off-resistance with two series oxide TFTs per cell
idea: Each cell uses two oxide TFTs in series on the same wordline, since glass area is cheap. The stack effect lowers off-state leakage, and one leaky transistor can no longer drain the cell.
why: Fact 3: both independent devices must be leaky for a cell to fail, which squares the tail probability (1e-6 to 1e-12), so refresh can be set by the median.

title: Asymmetric storage-node-side implant using U.S.-built ion implanters
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: a tilted, shadowed implant on domestically built implanters grades only the storage-node side of the access transistor with a light, deep LDD and no halo, while the bitline side keeps strong doping for drive current.
why: Lowers junction field and trap-assisted tunnelling at the storage node, the leakage-tail source, ~3-10x while keeping write speed, with all-domestic tooling.

title: Solera placement: weak rows host hot data refreshed by use
idea: In a solera the youngest wine sits in the most-handled barrels; map frequently activated pages onto rows with the worst measured retention, since each activation restores their charge more often than refresh would, and put cold pages on the strongest rows, which then get 4-8x longer refresh intervals.
why: Uses retention-tail rows (fact 3) instead of sparing them and cuts refresh on the cold majority; ~2-4x refresh reduction with no added cells.

title: Ionization-current strike sentinels trigger instant local scrub
idea: Effect: radiation-induced photoconductivity in silicon. A sparse large-area reverse-biased junction sentinel per mat collects the ionization charge of an alpha or neutron strike as a current spike; the controller then immediately read-corrects-writes only the rows within the strike radius instead of waiting for a whole-device patrol scrub.
why: Soft errors and ECC strength: multi-bit accumulation within one codeword is caught within microseconds, so lighter on-die ECC (~6% instead of 12.5% parity) or lower-Qcrit (weaker, smaller) cells become acceptable.

title: Eliminate domain switching: antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor biased at transition edge
idea: Anneal ALD ZrO2 at <=400 C into its antiferroelectric phase, and DC-bias the plate just below the field-induced AFE-to-FE transition, where small-signal permittivity peaks (k~50-70). Read and write swings stay inside the linear region, so domains never fully switch.
why: Reaches the k~70 needed to break the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) at low AR; avoiding switching removes ferroelectric fatigue, wake-up and imprint; BEOL-compatible capacitor for stacked arrays.

title: Population-coded bits: sixteen unreliable nanoparticle cells vote by current
idea: Synapses release vesicles with 10-90% probability yet neural populations are reliable; store each bit in ~16 spin-coated nanoparticle charge-trap sites under one coarse crosspoint, written together and read as summed current against a threshold, so up to ~5 dead or leaky sites never flip the bit.
why: Cost per GB: sites need no individual patterning, only relaxed-litho crosspoints, replacing precise devices with statistics; claimed ~100x cheaper per bit at ~3-5x latency.

title: Lifetime-typed allocation maps short-lived buffers to unrefreshed regions
idea: Timescale matching (data lifetime vs retention): the compiler/runtime tags each allocation with an expected lifetime (<1 ms, <64 ms, persistent) and the allocator places it in regions binned by retention. Short-lived buffers go to refresh-disabled or weak-cell regions that only have to hold data until it dies.
why: Cuts refresh energy (~16-33% of idle power) in AI workloads where most activations live under 10 ms, and gives weak-retention bins a use.

title: Whirlwind marginal checking reborn: live voltage-margin sweeps retire weak rows
idea: MIT Whirlwind and SAGE found dying tubes before they failed by deliberately lowering supply voltages during maintenance ('marginal checking'). The controller does this online: one subarray at a time is copied aside and exercised at VARY -60 mV, 4x stretched refresh and a skewed sense reference; any cell that fails under margin is logged and remapped before it can fail at nominal settings.
why: Retention tail and VRT (fact 3): catching marginal cells early lets the nominal refresh interval stretch 2-4x (refresh energy -50-75%) and lets vendors screen less aggressively at test; ~5-10% cost per bit from yield.

title: Outlet-store triage: route reject dies by failure type
idea: Adapted from garment outlets that sort irregulars by flaw type and sell each to a buyer who does not care about that flaw: dies that fail final test are classified on existing testers by signature (retention-weak, speed-weak, hammer-weak, stuck-bit) and packaged into matched products: retention-weak into high-refresh CXL tiers, speed-weak into low-clock edge devices, hammer-weak into read-mostly AI weight stores with low activation rates.
why: Yield and cost per bit (fact 4): each failure type is harmless in some workload; recovering 3-5% of currently scrapped dies adds bits from existing trailing and current lines with no new capacity.

title: Wafer-scale 180 nm DRAM with mesh self-routing around defects
idea: Ideal: 100% yield without a perfect fab. Closest: build an entire 200 mm wafer as one memory module of ~2,000 subarray tiles linked by a redundant mesh; a boot-time BIST disables bad tiles and soft-routes around them, so random defects only remove capacity and never kill the part.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: turns old 180 nm lines into high-capacity modules with no die sort, dicing or per-die packaging.

title: CD-ROM cross-interleaving to retire row and column redundancy
idea: Adapted from the CD's cross-interleaved Reed-Solomon code, which spreads each codeword along the disc so a scratch becomes many small correctable errors: each ECC codeword's symbols are mapped diagonally across 8 subarrays, 8 sub-wordline drivers and 8 local sense-amp stripes, so losing any one driver, stripe or column produces at most one symbol error per codeword.
why: Repair area and burst failures (fact 7): periphery defects that now need redundant drivers and fuses become routine single-symbol corrections, freeing ~2-4% die area and raising yield on large 32-64 Gb dies.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembled arrays with defect-mapped sparing replace EUV
idea: Effect: microphase separation of high-chi block copolymers. Sub-10 nm vertical-channel cell arrays are patterned by directed self-assembly, which is cheap but leaves ~1e-4 placement defects; instead of demanding litho-perfect arrays, each mat carries ~3% spare columns plus a post-fab electrical defect map and symbol ECC, so error tolerance absorbs the disorder.
why: 10x density: F ~7 nm (versus 12 nm) at 4F^2 is ~4.4x per layer, and 2-3 tiers give ~10x. Same cost: 5-7 EUV layers (depreciation ~55% of wafer cost) are replaced by spin-coat and anneal steps.

title: Wide-bandgap floating-body cell where intrinsic carriers vanish
idea: Floating-body cells lose stored holes by SRH generation, which scales with ni ~ exp(-Eg/2kT). 4H-SiC (3.26 eV) has ni ~1e-9 cm^-3 vs 1e10 in Si, ~1e19 lower. Store holes in a p-type SiC or GaN-2DHG floating body under an n-channel, write by band-to-band/impact-ionization pulse, and read by threshold shift.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): from ms toward seconds-hours with no capacitor. SiC substrates have a strong U.S. supply base.

title: Policy: glass-memory fabs qualified on raw BER plus mandated host ECC
idea: Fund new U.S. glass-substrate memory lines next to domestic glass makers, and back a JEDEC-style class that qualifies such memory on raw BER and retention with mandatory host-side ECC, instead of demanding near-perfect dies.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: weaker cells are accepted by standard, bringing memory onshore without EUV or silicon wafers.

title: Leaky rutile-TiO2 capacitors finally reach k near 80
idea: Po: a capacitor allowed to leak. Al-doped rutile TiO2 (k ~80-100) or SrTiO3 becomes the cell dielectric; it was rejected because its leakage tail breaks 64 ms retention, but with 1% BER tolerance that tail is acceptable.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): reaches the k ~70 target, keeping pillar AR at ~40-50:1 for the same Cs.

title: Spectral Goertzel detector spots periodic hammer patterns cheaply
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration/resonance: per-bank Goertzel filters run on hashed activation-address streams; a hammer loop shows up as a sharp spectral line at the attacker's loop frequency and triggers targeted neighbor refresh for the hashed rows.
why: Detects hammering with a few thousand gates instead of KB-scale per-row counter tables (~10x less area than per-row-counter tracking); a tiny counter covers aperiodic attacks.

title: Bain-marie phase-change heat buffer clipping DIMM temperature spikes
idea: A bain-marie holds food below 100 C. A paraffin or salt-hydrate PCM pouch melting at ~78-80 C is bonded into the DIMM heatspreader. During load bursts it absorbs latent heat and holds the dies below 85 C, so the 2x refresh rule never triggers. Off-the-shelf PCM, a thermal chamber and qualification fit in under 12 months and under $300k.
why: Avoiding 2x refresh in hot servers saves ~10% bandwidth and 16-33% of idle power (fact 3), and it keeps the retention tail in its nominal regime.

title: Federal commons for dead refresh-free memory IP plus shared qualification line
idea: Most refresh-free memory ventures (T-RAM, Z-RAM, Kilopass, Spin Memory and others) died less from physics than from missing reliability data and qualified second sources. Fix: a federal program buys or licenses their patent estates into an open pool and funds a shared U.S. qualification line that runs JEDEC-style retention, endurance, disturb and soft-error testing on every revived cell and publishes the failure-rate data.
why: Cuts years and tens of $M from each zero-refresh technology's path to qualification, lowering capital intensity and lifting U.S. manufacturability.

title: Substitute room-temperature DIMMs with sub-zero cold-plate memory loops
idea: Swap air cooling of DRAM for a dedicated dew-point-controlled liquid loop holding modules at about -10 C; leakage roughly halves per ~10 C, so retention rises ~8-10x and refresh intervals stretch, and tail-limited cells pass.
why: Refresh power (fact 3) drops ~80-90% and weak bins become usable; needs no change to the die.

title: Siberian engineer: sub-zero memory halls let leaky reject cells pass
idea: A Siberian engineer uses the climate as a component: run DRAM-heavy racks in -30 to -40 C glycol-immersion blocks that are free-cooled in cold regions; junction leakage falls ~2x per 10 C, so retention rises ~30-100x, and dies are tested and binned at that temperature so cells that fail at 85 C ship as 'cold-grade' parts.
why: Fact 3: refresh (16-33% of idle power) nearly vanishes, and low-temperature binning raises good-die yield and supply while slowing retention aging; condensation and cold start are the risks.

title: Writer-side stuck-at coding dodges defects instead of correcting them
idea: Po: the defects write the data. For stuck cells revealed by read-before-write, the encoder picks the coset of a partitioned linear code whose codeword matches the stuck values (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov defective-memory coding), so redundancy is about the defect fraction (~1%) rather than several times it.
why: Static 1% defects cost ~1-2% overhead instead of ~10%, so the defect tolerance itself costs ~5x less.

title: Twistor revival: thermally drawn memory fibre, reel-tested, bad segments skipped
idea: Bell's twistor memory stored bits along woven magnetic wires. Thermally draw a multi-material preform (glass or polymer cladding, embedded metal wordlines, a ferroelectric or charge-storing core) into kilometres of memory fibre in a fully dry process; a reel-to-reel tester maps bad segments the way tape drives map defects, and good segments are woven into mats addressed like twistor planes.
why: Water and capital (fact 4): fibre drawing needs no ultrapure-water wet cleans (>10x less water than a wafer flow) and little capital, and segment mapping makes a crude process usable; density and speed are far from DRAM-class today.

title: Iterative product codes with tiny hard-decision decoders
idea: Po: the code is a crossword puzzle. A 4 KB page is laid out as a 2D array protected by short BCH row and column component codes (like optical-transport staircase codes); a few rounds of iterative hard-decision decoding fix 1% BER at ~12-15% overhead.
why: Keeps 1%-BER memory affordable in power: ~10x less decoder energy than soft LDPC, well under 0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Eliminate EUV and single capacitors: self-assembled redundant capacitor fingers per bit
idea: Pattern capacitor holes at sub-20 nm pitch by directed self-assembly of a block copolymer annealed at ~250 C, and wire four cylinders in parallel per cell. A DSA defect that drops or merges one cylinder then only reduces Cs ~25% instead of killing the bit.
why: Makes DSA defectivity tolerable and removes EUV layers at the capacitor level (fact 4); cell yield follows per-quad rather than per-hole statistics.

title: Eliminate single-device leakage tails: two series oxide TFTs per cell
idea: Stack a second access TFT vertically over the first (no extra area in BEOL) with an independently formed gate stack. A cell leaks only if both devices are tail outliers, so the tail probability is squared (1e-6 becomes 1e-12).
why: Turns the worst-cell retention problem (fact 3) from a statistical tail into a near-impossible coincidence, so refresh intervals can be set by median cells, 10-100x longer.

title: Small-die tile DRAM on depreciated U.S. lines plus erasure coding
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation under the U.S.-only rule: dies are split into 1-2 Gb tiles made on fully depreciated, EUV-free domestic DRAM nodes, and many tiles are packaged at a U.S. OSAT with a U.S. logic die that rides through a dead tile with tile-level erasure coding.
why: Small dies yield higher and depreciated tools cut wafer cost ~40-50% (depreciation is ~55% of cost), so domestic bits get cheaper without new EUV fabs.

title: Contactless RF test coils make every die's retention map cheap
idea: Inverts 'test requires probe needles': one top-metal mask adds an on-die inductive coil and rectifier so whole wafers are powered and read wirelessly in parallel inside a heated chamber for hours of retention mapping without probe cards.
why: Cuts test cost (~10-15% of DRAM cost) and gives every die the full weak-cell map that tolerance schemes need.

title: IBM MXT compression repurposed only to make room for in-line ECC
idea: IBM's MXT memory compression (Pinnacle, 2001) died of latency and allocation complexity. Fix exactly that by compressing only enough to free 8-16 bytes per 64-byte line (fixed size, no reallocation) and storing a strong symbol code in the freed space, with incompressible lines falling back to a small parity region.
why: Chipkill-class protection on non-ECC x8/x16 DIMMs and LPDDR, so cheaper higher-BER parts can serve servers; ~12% capacity saved versus ECC DIMMs.

title: On-die microheaters anneal traps that cause leakage drift
idea: Worse: let interface traps and gate-oxide defects accumulate until leakage tails grow and retention collapses. Flip: embed polysilicon microheaters under each bank and, in scheduled maintenance windows with data migrated away, pulse local anneals to ~250 C for milliseconds to recover trap-assisted leakage, a self-healing service.
why: Aging and VRT (fact 3): periodic anneal could hold retention near time-zero, allowing less end-of-life guardband (~2x refresh relief) and longer service life.

title: Elastic spare rows borrowed from user capacity on demand
idea: Time shift (fab-time redundancy -> lifetime redundancy): instead of fixed spare rows burned at the fab, all rows ship as user capacity, and the controller later converts address-remapped rows into spares through a firmware remap table as wear and weak cells appear.
why: Recovers the ~2-4% of array area spent on idle redundancy at time zero and spends it only when needed.

title: Hotel keycard: polarity encoding minimizes charged cells; empty rows skip refresh
idea: Like lights cutting off when the keycard leaves, each line stores a polarity bit chosen to minimize physically charged cells, and rows whose cells are all discharged (zeroed or free pages) set a per-row flag that skips refresh entirely.
why: Only charged cells leak: at 125 C halving the charged population and exempting empty rows (often 20-40% of memory) slashes hot refresh energy and exposure over 10 years.

title: Dielectric-absorption reservoir backs up charge in tiny capacitors
idea: Effect: dielectric absorption (Debye relaxation, 'soakage'). The storage capacitor is a bilayer of thin fast high-k plus a slow polar layer with tau ~ms; on write the slow layer partially polarizes, and as leakage drains the fast charge, its relaxation current flows back into the node, stretching retention of a 0.5 fF cap several-fold. A two-step read (fast charge, then soaked charge) gives a second vote for marginal cells.
why: 10x density: 0.5 fF planar caps with ~3x retention extension stack 24 tiers at ~0.4x per-tier density (~10x). Same cost: the AR-75 pillar etch and its EUV patterning are removed.

title: Substitute permanent dielectric breakdown with self-healing anodizable capacitor dielectric
idea: Swap the static high-k stack for a high-k layer over an anodizable Al/Ta thin film inside a mild solid electrolyte layer, so a breakdown spot leaks current that locally re-anodizes the metal and seals the defect, like electrolytic-capacitor self-healing.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): self-healing allows a thinner, higher-field dielectric (~1.5x more charge per area) without killing yield on pinholes.

title: Zero added disturb at tighter pitch: buried electron-sink layer
idea: Imposed limit: shrink wordline pitch without adding disturbance. A thin carbon-doped or SiGe trap-rich layer is implanted beneath the buried wordlines. It captures and recombines electrons injected by repeated aggressor activation before they diffuse to neighboring storage-node junctions.
why: Fact 9: could raise hammer thresholds several-fold and allow the 6F^2 pitch to keep shrinking without pushing thresholds below 1k.

title: Twice the bits, same capacitor: trellis-coded four-level cells
idea: Imposed limit: double the bits without a bigger capacitor. Each cell stores 4 charge levels and raw BER of ~1e-3 is accepted. Trellis-coded modulation across 8 cells (as in modems) adds structured redundancy, and the set is decoded by a Viterbi block in the sense-amp periphery.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: ~1.7x net bits per cell after coding overhead with no new capacitor geometry.

title: Substitute per-line ECC with row-long LDPC using wasted page overfetch
idea: Since every activation loads an 8 KB row anyway (fact 8), add a long LDPC codeword over the whole row, decoded during refresh and scrub cycles, plus a light per-line code for fast reads; long codes reach about 3% overhead at raw BER near 1e-3.
why: Turns the 128x overfetch into correction context: tolerates cells ~100x weaker than today, enabling smaller capacitors or higher-AR-free cells (fact 1).

title: Page-wide LDPC computed in the sense-amp stripe
idea: Ideal: error correction with zero overhead bits. Closest: since every activate already senses an ~8 kb row, add a long-block LDPC code over the whole row (~3% parity versus 12.5% for per-word SECDED) decoded bit-serially in the sense-amp stripe during tRAS, so dozens of marginal cells per row are fixed before any column read.
why: Facts 1, 3, 8: turns the 128x overfetch into an asset; tolerates ~100x higher raw BER at lower parity cost, letting Cs drop ~30% or refresh slow 4-8x.

title: B: boron-10 hBN coating shields DIMMs from thermal neutrons
idea: A small coating line sprays an epoxy loaded with 10B-enriched hexagonal boron nitride flakes over DRAM packages on DIMMs and HBM modules; 10B absorbs thermal neutrons before they reach residual 10B in die dielectrics, and hBN spreads heat. Needs only mixing, a spray booth and a cure oven.
why: Cuts the thermal-neutron share of soft errors (large near concrete and water-rich datacenters), letting operators relax scrub rate or ECC strength.

title: Substitute victim refresh with an in-die hot-row cache absorbing aggressors
idea: Replace 'refresh the neighbors' with 'stop hammering': a small SRAM row cache per bank catches rows activated more than N times in a window, so further accesses hit the cache and the array wordline stops toggling.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) plus energy: removes hammer stress at the source and saves activation energy on hot rows ~20-30%.

title: One end-to-end codeword spans array, link and controller
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: low-margin | integration: DIMM or CXL with host-side decoder | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. The host encodes once with a strong LDPC and the DRAM stores and returns the raw codeword with no on-die ECC or link CRC, so one parity budget absorbs both ~1e-4 errors from a 0.45 V array and errors from a ~100 mV-swing link.
why: Constraint/Fact 5: I/O energy (dominant in DDR5's 10-20 pJ/bit) and array CV^2 both drop ~4-5x, ~10x combined, and on-die ECC logic disappears.

title: Hadamard-spread weight storage turns bit flips into tiny noise
idea: One exponent or MSB flip in BF16/INT8 weights can wreck a model, which forces DRAM-grade BER. Store each block of 64 weights after a 64-point Walsh-Hadamard transform, invertible in the accelerator for <1% compute. A single stored-bit flip then spreads as +/-delta/8 across 64 weights, below model noise.
why: Error tolerance: inference weights can live at raw BER ~1e-6, i.e., ~10x slower refresh or weak dies, for most AI memory footprint.

title: ECC-cluster feedback trims individual sense-amp offsets
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: when correctable errors cluster on one bitline, the controller writes a per-sense-amp offset trim (small capacitor or back-bias DAC loaded from a trim RAM), fixing the weak-sense-amp part of the tail instead of sparing the column.
why: Much of the effective retention tail is SA offset, not cell leakage; trimming lets ~10-20% smaller signal (smaller Cs) be sensed reliably and saves spare columns.

title: Intermittent-IoT rebuild: refresh-free weights refetched from flash on CRC fail
idea: Energy-harvesting IoT nodes let volatile state die and rebuild it from nonvolatile checkpoints. Apply that to immutable LLM weights: refresh the weight region only every 1-4 s (most cells retain seconds), give each 4 KB page a CRC-32 checked on read, and silently re-DMA any failing page from the golden copy on SSD or flash. This needs a per-region refresh-interval register.
why: Weights are ~50-80% of inference memory. Cutting their refresh 16-64x removes most refresh power and bandwidth for that footprint, and lets weight memory use retention-reject dies (fact 3).

title: Telecom regenerator: 65nm DIMM coprocessor for refresh and hammer defense
idea: Adapted from optical-network regenerators that clean signals in-line without the endpoints knowing: a small 65 nm chip beside the register clock driver snoops the command/address bus, keeps approximate per-row activation counts in SRAM, and injects targeted refresh-management commands and retention-aware refresh skipping on the module itself, independent of the host controller.
why: Row hammer and refresh (facts 3, 9): moves mitigation off the leading-edge DRAM die and off the host, so older DRAM dies without in-DRAM counters can serve securely; built entirely in mature logic fabs.

title: Fire sprinkler: margin-sniffing sense amps trigger local auto-repair
idea: A second, offset-biased comparator per sense-amp group flags any activate whose bitline differential is under ~40 mV; flagged rows are immediately re-restored and logged on-die, and repeat offenders are remapped through soft PPR with no host involvement - a sprinkler that fires only where the heat is.
why: Catches weakening cells (retention, VRT, hammer) before they flip, making every read a free audit; supports ~2x longer refresh and smaller Cs margins.

title: Red-team defense: keyed, re-randomized row scrambling inside the DRAM
idea: Treat the row-hammer attacker as the extreme user. Inside each subarray, the DRAM maps logical rows to physical rows through a lightweight keyed permutation (a 4-round Feistel on the row bits). The key is re-drawn at each boot and rotated gradually by background migration during self-refresh, so attackers cannot learn which rows are physical neighbours. External addressing and timing stay standard.
why: Targeted hammering depends on knowing the neighbours. Randomizing them turns attacks into low-odds guessing, so vendors can tolerate cells that flip near 1k activations without heavy per-row counters (fact 9).

title: Vacuum-tube getter flash revived: sacrificial getter soaks recycled-water metals
idea: Vacuum tubes carried a barium getter, flashed after sealing, that soaked up residual gas for the tube's whole life. A sacrificial gettering layer (carbon/phosphorus co-implant or a polysilicon sink) under each array, plus a final low-temperature 'getter flash' anneal, pulls Fe, Cu and Ni away from storage junctions, so trace metals from lower-purity recycled rinse water never reach the cells.
why: Water: makes a ~90-95% closed rinse loop at 1-5 MOhm-cm acceptable (~10x less fresh water) by shielding the retention tail (fact 3) from the metals that loop carries.

title: Row-embedded fault patch list replaces fuse repair
idea: Rearrange repair data into the row it fixes: each 8 Kb row reserves ~32 bits holding up to two (column-address, correct-bit) patches, and the column path applies them on the fly at read, fixing single-cell defects without spare rows or fuses.
why: Single-cell hard faults dominate yield loss; in-row patching cuts redundancy area and lets ~10x higher single-cell defect density ship.

title: Ar: argon-implanted recombination layer annihilates stray carriers below cells
idea: Implant argon deep below the active cell region to form a thin damaged layer with short minority-carrier lifetime (the IGBT lifetime-control trick), placed outside junction depletion regions, so substrate electrons recombine before diffusing to storage nodes.
why: Cuts substrate-mediated row hammer (fact 9) and alpha/neutron charge collection; claim ~3x lower soft-error rate, letting weaker Cs pass.

title: National DRAM failure-telemetry exchange feeds back to U.S. fabs
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback at national scale: a CHIPS-funded, privacy-scrubbed exchange pools corrected-error, hammer and retention telemetry from U.S. hyperscalers per die lot, returning per-lot refresh/hammer settings to deployed systems and process-shift alerts to U.S. fabs.
why: Closes the field-to-fab loop: ~2x per-lot refresh relaxation and faster yield learning for domestic DRAM ramps (months saved against fact-4 capital timelines).

title: Holographic page spreading: Hadamard-encode weights so failures become noise
idea: 1970s holographic memories spread every bit across the whole plate, so a scratch only added noise. Before writing neural-network weight pages, a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform is applied across each 2 KB block; dead bitlines, hammered regions or retention clusters then come back after the inverse transform as low-amplitude noise spread over all weights, which models tolerate without ECC.
why: Error tolerance for the largest AI capacity tier: removes 12.5% ECC overhead and repair for weight memory and tolerates clustered faults, for ~log2(N) adds per value in the base die.

title: Minutes-retention trap-charge cell with age-stamped scrubbing
idea: Box [medium: charge in SiN trap layer behind ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide | access: 1T gate-coupled storage | sense: Vt current sense | integration: 3D vertical stack | substrate: bulk | fab: NAND-style tools, no EUV]. Bits are written by low-voltage direct tunneling in nanoseconds and retained for minutes; reads sense transistor Vt without disturbing charge, and each block carries an age stamp so only blocks nearing their retention budget are scrubbed.
why: Constraint: a read is a small current pulse on a short line with no restore, ~10x below ACT+restore; refresh ~1000x rarer.

title: Fleet error telemetry sold back to fabs to shave guardbands
idea: Worse: hyperscalers hoard corrected-error logs while DRAM makers set guardbands blind. Flip: a data-exchange business in which cloud operators sell anonymized per-die error and temperature histories, keyed to die IDs, to manufacturers, who use the field evidence to relax test limits and requalify borderline bins.
why: Yield and test cost: real field-failure data can justify recovering several percent of dies now scrapped for guardband margin, adding supply with zero capex.

title: Fleet error telemetry redeploys aging DIMMs instead of scrapping
idea: Ideal: no DIMM is ever retired early. Closest: hyperscalers pool corrected-error telemetry (per row, bank, temperature) to predict which DIMMs are degrading, then move them to error-tolerant services (caches, AI inference with retries) under stricter scrubbing rather than replacing them, stretching service life from ~5 to ~8 years.
why: Supply axis: effectively adds 20-40% to installed DRAM capacity over a hardware cycle with zero fab capex.

title: Spectral activation listener detects hammer rhythms without row counters
idea: Po: the attacker sings, so listen for the song. A few Goertzel/sliding-DFT filters per bank analyze the time series of activated row-address bits; hammering shows up as sharp periodic peaks, which trigger targeted refresh of rows matching the peak's address hash, replacing large per-row counter tables.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) at ~1k thresholds, where counter SRAM becomes prohibitive: mitigation logic area down ~10x versus per-row counters.

title: Ca: bone-remodeling scrubber resorbs and rebuilds rows by stress
idea: Controller firmware runs osteoclast/osteoblast loops: scrub rate per region scales with its access stress (Wolff's law), rows whose corrected-error rate climbs are resorbed (data migrated, row retired via PPR or OS page offlining) and spare capacity is rebuilt.
why: Self-healing lets weaker DIMMs serve full lives; targets ~10x fewer uncorrectable errors than fixed-rate scrub at equal scrub bandwidth.

title: Substitute stuck-cell loss with coset coding that writes on dirty paper
idea: When NV cells wear to stuck-at values, the encoder picks among 2^k coset representatives of each data word the one that agrees with known stuck cells (Gelfand-Pinsker 'dirty paper' coding), so dead cells still store bits correctly.
why: Endurance (DRAM-class needs effectively unlimited): extends usable life of ReRAM/PCM arrays ~10-100x past first stuck cell at a few % overhead.

title: Oersted-pushed magnetic domain wall counts activations per row
idea: Effect: field-driven domain-wall motion. A short perpendicular-magnetized CoFeB nanowire with ~64 pinning notches runs alongside each wordline driver; each activation current pulse's Oersted field advances a domain wall one notch, and when the wall reaches the last notch a small MTJ senses it, requests neighbor refresh and a reverse pulse rewinds the wall. The count is exact and non-volatile, and it is built in BEOL over the driver.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row activation counts with zero SRAM area and no loss at power-down or self-refresh entry; avoids the 10-20% bandwidth cost of conservative probabilistic mitigations.

title: Tempered write: overdriven restore for rows predicted to idle
idea: Tempered glass is pre-stressed to resist cracking; when the controller predicts a row will sit idle (freshly written cold data), it issues a 'tempered' restore with boosted array voltage or longer write-recovery from a pump, storing ~20-30% more charge so the row can skip several refresh cycles.
why: Extends retention of idle data and reduces refresh count (fact 3) at the cost of rare high-energy writes; ~1.5-2x refresh reduction for cold memory.

title: Buried electron-sink line between rows soaks up hammer charge
idea: Give hammer electrons somewhere else to go: a shallow trench cut with HBr/Cl2 (no fluorocarbons) between adjacent rows is filled with in-situ boron-doped epi (avoiding fluorine-bearing BF2 implants) and biased slightly positive to collect migrating electrons before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Row hammer threshold possibly raised 10x+ without counters or refresh; costs ~5-10% cell area.

title: Carbon-doped gettering liner between rows traps migrating electrons
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: vertical channel | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk with carbon-implanted isolation liner | fab: DUV implant]. The isolation between adjacent rows is lined with carbon-doped silicon that creates recombination centres >50 nm from storage junctions, so electrons injected by a toggling aggressor recombine before reaching the victim node.
why: Fact 9: raises hammer threshold ~5-10x passively; the risk is adding retention tail, controlled by keeping the liner away from junctions.

title: Si: silicon-on-nothing voids block substrate electron migration between rows
idea: Form empty-space-in-silicon cavities (trench array plus hydrogen-anneal surface migration) under the storage-node regions so electrons released during aggressor wordline cycling cannot diffuse through the substrate to neighbor storage nodes, while junction volume (generation leakage) shrinks.
why: Cuts the charge-migration row-hammer path (fact 9) and the junction-leakage tail (fact 3); could raise the hammer threshold ~10x.

title: STT-MRAM asymmetric write errors absorbed by Z-channel codes
idea: STT-MRAM lost the DRAM-replacement race partly because write error rate demands high current, and failures are strongly one-directional (P to AP). Fix: deliberately lower write current until errors are almost purely in that direction, then protect with asymmetric Z-channel codes (Varshamov/Constantin-Rao style) that correct only that direction.
why: ~30% lower write current/energy or ~40% less parity at equal uncorrectable rate; a smaller access transistor raises density.

title: Substitute TiN electrodes with conductive-oxide electrodes for fatigue-free HZO
idea: Replace TiN electrodes on HfZrO ferroelectric capacitors with oxide electrodes (RuO2, IrO2 or indium-free LaNiO3) that act as oxygen-vacancy sinks, the same fix that removed fatigue in PZT FeRAM.
why: Endurance from ~1e11 toward >1e14 cycles makes FeRAM close to DRAM-class endurance; LaNiO3 avoids platinum-group scarcity.

title: Macronix self-healing heater idea reborn as wordline Joule annealing
idea: Macronix's 2012 self-healing flash (on-chip heaters annealing oxide traps) never shipped because dedicated heaters cost area and power. Fix: use the existing buried wordline itself as the heater, so rows that ECC or scrubbing flag for rising leakage get millisecond high-current pulses that anneal the access-transistor interface traps driving the leakage tail.
why: In-field self-healing of retention and hammer-induced trap damage; shrinks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) over life instead of letting it grow, enabling longer refresh intervals.

title: Per-row ferroelectric Vt trim of access transistors lowers wordline swing
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: FeFET access transistor with HZO gate layer | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. At test and periodically in the field, each row's access-transistor Vt is trimmed by partially polarizing its ferroelectric gate, pulling leaky-tail rows up and slow rows down, so the wordline can swing ~1.3 V instead of ~3 V without a leakage tail.
why: Constraint: wordline CV^2 ~5x lower and the VPP pump removed, ~10x on the wordline path; Fact 3: leakage tail compressed by trimming.

title: Wavelength-addressed optical wordlines open single row segments
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: Ge photo-FET | sense: standard | integration: SiN waveguide wordlines with ring filters | substrate: SOI | fab: DUV]. Each row is opened by light: a waveguide over the row carries several wavelengths and ring filters steer each wavelength to one 64-bit segment of photo-gated access devices, so there is no high-voltage wordline swing and no capacitive wordline-to-wordline coupling.
why: Constraint: removes ~3 V wordline CV^2 and pump loss and fetches only one segment, ~10x per useful bit; Fact 9: kills the wordline-coupling component of row hammer.

title: Low-Vt access transistors cut the wordline swing to 2 V
idea: Po: let the transistor leak. The access-transistor threshold is lowered ~0.3 V, so the wordline boost drops from ~3 V to ~2 V and the negative standby bias shrinks; the leakage tail grows until ~1% of cells fail retention within the window, which the code absorbs.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline CV^2 energy down ~55%, smaller charge pumps (periphery, fact 7) and lower gate-oxide stress.

title: Dual-threshold sense amps feed soft-decision LDPC
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM read is a hard 0/1 decision': each sense amp gets a second offset comparator that flags weak-0/weak-1 when bitline signal is near the reference, giving NAND-style soft information; a soft-decision LDPC uses it to correct ~2x more errors per parity bit.
why: Cells can run with 30-40% less signal margin (smaller Cs, longer refresh; facts 1, 3) for a small periphery cost.

title: Thermal moat isolates the cool array from hot periphery
idea: Inverts 'the whole die shares one temperature': a single mask etches an air-gapped ring trench between the array and the hot periphery and I/O, forcing periphery heat to flow to the backside instead of laterally through the array.
why: Array runs ~8-10 C cooler, roughly doubling retention (fact 3) and halving refresh; also widens hammer margins.

title: pH-buffer storage node: antiferroelectric plateau resists leakage droop
idea: Adapted from chemical buffer solutions, which hold pH nearly constant by drawing on a reservoir as acid is added: add an antiferroelectric layer (Zr-rich HfZrO tuned so its field-induced transition sits just below VARY) in the storage capacitor, so leakage first drains the stored polarization reservoir while node voltage stays flat near the plateau, delaying the fall below the sense threshold.
why: Retention tail and charge wall (facts 1, 3): an effective Q-V plateau could give 3-5x more charge per volt near the operating point, extending retention 3-5x or allowing a much shorter capacitor.

title: Avalanche-gain gated diode preamplifies weak cell charge
idea: Effect: impact-ionization avalanche multiplication. A gated p-i-n diode at each sense node, biased just below breakdown and stabilized by a replica-diode bias loop, multiplies the small charge transferred from a weak cell ~10x (like an APD) before the latch sense amp resolves.
why: Makes 3-5x smaller signals readable, so leakier or smaller capacitors are acceptable, or bitlines can be longer with fewer sense amps (fact 7).

title: Battery-management Kalman estimator of per-region cell charge
idea: A BMS estimates a battery's state of charge with a Kalman filter. The memory controller runs a lightweight filter per region. Its inputs are temperature telemetry, the access history (every access restores charge) and occasional sentinel-read measurements. Refresh is issued only when the lower confidence bound of the estimated charge approaches the sense threshold.
why: Refresh costs ~46 fJ/bit and 16-33% of idle power (fact 3). Model-based refresh with a bounded error probability could cut it by 50-75%.

title: Wine-cellar memory: cold-plate DIMM sleds that multiply retention
idea: Adapted from cold-chain storage, where lowering temperature slows spoilage exponentially: memory sleds use existing data-center liquid cold plates to hold DRAM at 35-45 C instead of 70-85 C, and controllers drop to the longer refresh interval valid at low temperature, which also lets leakier, cheaper die bins qualify.
why: Refresh and retention tail (fact 3): leakage roughly halves every ~10 C, so a 30-40 C drop gives ~8-16x retention margin; refresh energy and bandwidth loss can fall up to ~75% and lower-grade dies become usable.

title: Base-die patch cache repairs any core die's weak cells
idea: Worse: give each core die a fixed, fused spare-row budget, so one unlucky die runs out of spares while its neighbors waste theirs. Flip: put a small SRAM patch cache plus address CAM on the HBM base logic die that serves correct data for weak rows of any core die, loaded at boot from a stored repair map and updatable in the field.
why: Facts 6-7: pools repair resources across the stack, raising stack yield and allowing core dies with fewer on-die spares and smaller periphery.

title: Cybersecurity honeypots: decoy rows tripwire hammering in real time
idea: Adapted from honeypots and canary tokens in network security: the OS seeds each bank with decoy pages holding known patterns physically adjacent to rows owned by untrusted tenants; a high-rate scrubber reads only the decoys, and any flip in a decoy pinpoints the aggressor rows for migration and tenant throttling.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): deterministic detection on existing DRAM without counters, spending ~1% capacity on decoys and focusing scrub bandwidth on <1% of rows.

title: Immunologist's fever: ECC strength rises with temperature, not refresh rate
idea: The body runs a fever to fight infection instead of working harder everywhere: above 85 C the controller switches marked regions from SECDED to a stronger BCH code, using adjacent capacity the OS reserved in advance, instead of doubling refresh across the whole device.
why: Fact 3: avoids 2x-refresh mode (10-20% bandwidth at high density), and only cold-tolerant capacity is borrowed.

title: CD-style cross-interleaved two-level code across banks
idea: CDs survive 2.5 mm scratches with CIRC: two Reed-Solomon codes plus delay interleaving. In the FPGA controller, an inner RS code per 64 B burst detects and flags errors. An outer RS code spans 28 lines that address-mapping skew places in different banks and subarrays. A hammered row or dead wordline, the 'scratch', then corrupts at most one symbol per outer codeword.
why: Survives whole-row and wordline failures at ~12% overhead, so chips can ship with fewer row spares and weaker hammer margins (fact 9).

title: Farmer's companion planting: cluster hot rows so neighbors self-refresh
idea: A farmer plants crops that protect each other: the OS or hypervisor uses per-page activation counters to put frequently activated pages in physically adjacent rows, because each activation restores a row's own charge; hot rows then hammer only other hot rows that are constantly restored, and rarely touched data is kept out of hot neighborhoods.
why: Fact 9 row hammer: removes most vulnerable aggressor-victim pairs without TRR logic or extra refreshes; matters most once thresholds fall below 1k activations.

title: Adiabatic charge-recycling refresh between subarray bitlines
idea: The physical minimum for refresh is the leaked charge times V (~0.1 fJ/bit), yet ~90% of the 46 fJ goes into swinging bitlines (Cbl ~10x Cs). Ramp the bitlines with an N-step adiabatic driver, then pass the charge on the restored bitlines to the next subarray's bitlines over a stepwise charge-share bus, so each refresh reuses ~70% of the previous swing.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): ~46 fJ/bit to ~12 fJ/bit, a 10-20% cut in idle power.
